blocks.title: In the curriculum

blocks.text: Statistics is about answering questions with data. At Stage 6 you plan your own small investigation, collect the right kind of data, record it neatly and choose a diagram that shows it clearly. The next page (Mode, Median, Mean and Range) shows how to describe and interpret the data you collect.

blocks.text: 1. Planning an investigation

A statistical investigation follows a cycle. You start with a **question**, and at the end you check whether your **prediction** was right. Usually you investigate a **set of related questions** — one main question split into smaller questions that you can answer with data.

items: **Ask** the main question and the related questions. Example — main question: “Do older students sleep less on school nights?” Related questions: How long do Stage 3 students sleep? How long do Stage 6 students sleep? Is there a big difference between students in the same stage?
**Predict**: “I think Stage 6 students sleep about 1 hour less than Stage 3 students.”
**Plan the data**: What will you collect (hours of sleep — continuous data)? From whom (for example 20 students from each stage)? How (a questionnaire for parents, or a sleep diary for one week)?
**Collect** and **record** the data in a tally chart or table.
**Represent** the data in a suitable diagram.
**Interpret**: describe what the data shows, answer each question, and **check your prediction**.

blocks.text: **Good planning tips:** ask enough people (a few answers can be misleading); ask the same question in the same way to everyone; for measurements, decide the unit and how accurate to be (e.g. to the nearest centimetre); and make sure the people you ask fit the question (ask Stage 6 students about Stage 6, not your family).
2. Three types of data

rows: favourite fruit, eye colour, type of pet, way to travel to school
the answer is a word or a group
numbers you **count**; only certain values are possible
number of brothers and sisters, goals in a match, shoe size, number of cars passing
you can’t have values in between, e.g. 2.5 siblings
numbers you **measure**; any value in a range is possible
height, mass, time to run 50 m, temperature, length of a leaf
you use a ruler, scales, a stopwatch or a thermometer

blocks.title: Shoe size is a trick question
blocks.text: Shoe size is measured from your foot, but shoe sizes only come in certain values (35, 36, 37…). So shoe size is **discrete**. Your actual foot length (e.g. 22.4 cm) is continuous.
3. Tally charts and frequency tables

A **tally chart** is the quickest way to record data as you collect it: draw one stroke for each answer and draw every fifth stroke across the four before it, so the marks come in groups of five that are easy to count. The **frequency** is the total for each row. A frequency table shows the frequencies as numbers.

Always check the total: 8 + 5 + 11 + 6 = 30, the number of students asked. For **continuous data**, use groups (class intervals) that do not overlap, for example 130 ≤ h < 135, 135 ≤ h < 140… A height of exactly 135 cm goes in the group 135 ≤ h < 140, because “135 ≤ h” includes 135 but “h < 135” does not.
4. Venn diagrams and Carroll diagrams (sorting)

Both diagrams **sort** items using two properties. In a **Venn diagram**, each circle is one property. Items with both properties go in the **overlap**; items with neither go **outside** the circles but inside the rectangle.

5. Bar charts

Use a **bar chart** for categorical data or discrete data. Each bar shows a frequency. The bars are the same width and have **gaps** between them. A good bar chart has a title, labels on both axes and a scale with equal steps that starts at 0.

6. Waffle diagrams and pie charts (parts of a whole)

Use these when you want to show how a whole is **split into parts** — proportions. A **waffle diagram** is a 10 × 10 grid of 100 squares, so **each square is 1%**. Count the squares of one colour to get the percentage.

blocks.caption: How 100 students travel to school. Bus has 45 squares, so 45% travel by bus. Bus and car together: 45% + 30% = 75%, that is three quarters.

blocks.text: A **pie chart** is a circle split into sectors. The whole circle is all the data. Half the circle is half the data; a quarter (a right angle at the centre) is a quarter of the data. To find a number of people, find that fraction of the total.

blocks.title: Comparing two pie charts
blocks.text: A bigger sector does not always mean more people. If one pie chart shows 24 students and another shows 200 students, a quarter of the second chart is 50 people, but a quarter of the first is only 6. Always check the totals.
7. Frequency diagrams for continuous data

For grouped **continuous** data (heights, times, masses) we draw a **frequency diagram**. It looks like a bar chart, but the bars **touch** because there are no gaps between the groups — every value from 130 cm to 155 cm belongs in some group. The horizontal axis is a number scale, like a ruler.

Use a **line graph** to show how something **changes over time**, when the measurement is continuous (temperature, height of a plant, distance travelled). Plot each reading as a cross, then join the crosses with straight lines. Time always goes on the horizontal axis.

9. Scatter graphs

A **scatter graph** shows whether there is a **relationship between two sets of measurements** taken from the same people or things. Each cross is one student: across for height, up for hand span. The points are **not** joined.

A **dot plot** shows each piece of discrete (or small numerical) data as one dot above a number line. It is quick to draw and you can still see every value, so it is good for small data sets.

blocks.text: 11. Choosing the best representation

rows: sorting numbers or shapes by two properties
shows which items have one, both or neither property
counting answers as you collect them
quick to record, easy to total
bar chart (or dot plot for small sets)
bar heights are easy to compare
showing parts of a whole / percentages
shows the proportion of each part
bars touch because the scale is continuous
shows rises and falls; you can read between points
is there a relationship between two measurements?
the pattern of crosses shows the relationship

blocks.title: بالعربي: نختار أي رسم؟
items: بيانات وصفية (ألوان، رياضات) أو بيانات معدودة → أعمدة بيانية (bar chart) بينها مسافات.
بيانات مقاسة ومجمّعة (أطوال، أزمنة) → frequency diagram والأعمدة ملزوقة في بعض.
تغيّر مع الوقت (درجة الحرارة طول اليوم) → line graph.
أجزاء من كل (نسب مئوية) → waffle diagram (كل مربع = 1%) أو pie chart.
هل في علاقة بين قياسين (الطول وطول الكف)؟ → scatter graph، والنقط ما بتتوصلش.

blocks.text: Worked examples

**Worked example 1** — Types of data  [2 marks]
Write whether each set of data is categorical, discrete or continuous: (a) the mass of each student’s school bag; (b) the number of goals each team scored; (c) each student’s favourite subject; (d) the time each student takes to walk to school.

rows: Is the answer a word? Yes

blocks.text:
**Answer:** (a) continuous, (b) discrete, (c) categorical, (d) continuous. 2 marks for all four, 1 mark for three correct.
**Common mistake:** calling every set of numbers “discrete”. Ask: was it **counted** or **measured**?

**Worked example 2** — Completing a frequency table  [2 marks]
40 students chose their favourite colour. Red 9, blue 13, green ?, yellow 6. (a) How many chose green? (b) Which colour was the mode (the most popular)?

items: Add the known frequencies: 9 + 13 + 6 = 28.
Subtract from the total: 40 − 28 = 12 chose green.
Compare: blue 13 is the largest frequency.

blocks.text:
**Worked example 3** — Carroll diagram  [1 mark]
A Carroll diagram has columns “has a right angle” / “has no right angle” and rows “quadrilateral” / “not a quadrilateral”. Write where these shapes go: square, right-angled triangle, rhombus (not a square), equilateral triangle.

**Method:** take each shape and answer both questions. Square: 4 sides (quadrilateral) and right angles → top-left. A rhombus that is not a square has no right angles → top-right. Each shape goes in exactly **one** cell.

**Worked example 4** — Waffle diagram  [2 marks]
Use the waffle diagram of how 100 students travel to school (section 6). (a) What percentage of students walk or cycle? (b) In the whole school 600 students travel in the same proportions. How many travel by car?

**Answer:** (a) 25% (b) 180 students.
**Common mistake:** answering “30” for part (b). 30 is the percentage (30 out of 100), not the number of students out of 600.

**Worked example 5** — Choosing a graph  [2 marks]
Amira measured the height of a bean plant every Monday for 8 weeks. Ali measured the heights of 30 bean plants on one day and grouped them. Which type of graph should each of them draw? Explain.

items: Amira: one plant, measured **over time** → **line graph**, because it shows how the height changes from week to week and she can read heights between the Mondays.
Ali: many measurements of continuous data, **grouped** → **frequency diagram** with touching bars, because height is continuous so the groups have no gaps.

blocks.text: **Exam technique:** in “explain” questions, name the graph **and** give a reason linked to the data (“because the data is continuous” / “because it shows change over time”).

**Worked example 6** — Planning an investigation  [2 marks]
Youssef wants to find out: “Do students who read more books get higher spelling scores?” (a) Write a prediction. (b) What data should he collect, and which graph should he draw?

items: (a) Prediction: “Students who read more books each month will get higher spelling scores.”

(b) For each student he needs **two** pieces of data: the number of books read in a month (discrete) and the spelling test score (discrete). He should ask a good number of students, for example the whole class.
Two measurements for each student, looking for a relationship → **scatter graph**.

blocks.text: **Answer:** prediction as above; collect books read and test score for each student; a scatter graph. If the crosses go up from left to right, his prediction is supported.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Mixing up discrete (counted) and continuous (measured) data.
Leaving gaps between the bars of a frequency diagram for continuous data — or no gaps in a bar chart for categories.
Reading a scale wrongly: always work out what one small step is worth before reading a bar.
Putting an item in both sides of a Carroll diagram, or in a Venn circle when it belongs in the overlap.
Forgetting that a value on the boundary, like 140 cm, belongs to the group 140 ≤ h < 145.
Joining the points on a scatter graph, or drawing a line graph for categorical data.
Giving a percentage when the question asks for a number of people (or the other way round).

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: “Complete the frequency table” or “complete the bar chart” — use a ruler and draw the bar exactly to the scale.
“Write these numbers in the correct place on the Venn diagram / Carroll diagram.”
“Is this data categorical, discrete or continuous?”
“Which graph would be best to show …? Explain your answer.”
Reading questions: “How many more…”, “What percentage…”, “What fraction of the pie chart…”.
“Write one more question Ahmed could ask in his investigation” or “Was the prediction correct? Use the data to explain.”

blocks.title: قاعدة لازم تحفظها
items: اسأل نفسك: الإجابة كلمة؟ → categorical. رقم بنعدّه؟ → discrete. رقم بنقيسه بأداة قياس؟ → continuous.
قبل ما تقرأ أي رسم: شوف المقياس — كل خط يساوي كام؟
في الـ waffle diagram كل مربع = 1% من 100 مربع.

questions.q: Which graph is best for showing how the temperature in a classroom changed during one day?
questions.e: Temperature is continuous and is changing over time, so a line graph is best: it shows the rises and falls and you can read between the readings.

questions.q: Nour wants to investigate: “Do Stage 6 students spend more time on homework than Stage 4 students?” (a) Write a prediction. (b) Describe what data she should collect and how. (c) Name a suitable way to show her results.
questions.ms: 1 mark: a sensible prediction linked to the question (e.g. “Stage 6 students spend more time on homework”). 1 mark: collect the time spent on homework (e.g. minutes per day or per week) from a fair number of students in each stage, e.g. by a questionnaire or a homework diary; must mention both stages. 1 mark: a suitable representation, e.g. two frequency diagrams with the same groups, or a dual bar chart of grouped times, or two dot plots; accept a table of averages compared. Do not accept a pie chart alone or a scatter graph.
questions.e: Prediction: “Stage 6 students spend more time on homework each day than Stage 4 students.” Data: the number of minutes each student spends on homework per day, from (say) 20 students in Stage 4 and 20 in Stage 6, using a short questionnaire or a one-week diary. Time is continuous, so group the times (e.g. 0 ≤ t < 15, 15 ≤ t < 30 …) and draw a frequency diagram for each stage on the same scale, then compare.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Plan first: question → prediction → what data, from whom, how → collect → represent → interpret and check the prediction.
Categorical = words; discrete = counted; continuous = measured.
Bar charts have gaps; frequency diagrams for continuous data have touching bars.
Line graph = change over time; scatter graph = relationship between two measurements; waffle/pie = parts of a whole.
Before reading any graph, check the scale: what is one step worth?
